case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: The court decided standing, not the outer definition of authorship, and it addressed an animal rather than a system a human directs. It answers who cannot own a work, not who does.
case.holding: A crested macaque that took photographs of itself lacked statutory standing under the Copyright Act, because the Act's terms presume human authors and next-of-kin, and a non-human cannot sue for infringement of works it created.

live_cases.name: University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC

case.why_ai_cites_it: The monkey-selfie case is the closest appellate authority that a non-human creator has no rights in what it makes. It is cited to establish that model outputs have no author of their own, which cuts for AI companies when they disclaim ownership and against anyone trying to anchor rights in the machine itself.

reading.body:
The clearest appellate signal on non-human authorship is that a creator outside the human species cannot sue under the Copyright Act, and AI practitioners cite this to argue that model outputs have no author of their own.

The Ninth Circuit's holding in *Naruto v. Slater* turned on statutory standing, not on a comprehensive definition of authorship. The court found that the Copyright Act's terms, including provisions for next-of-kin, presuppose human authors, so a crested macaque had no right to bring an infringement claim. The reasoning did not address AI systems, which differ from animals in that a human directs their operation, but the case is the closest appellate authority available for the proposition that non-human creation produces no rights-holder on the creating side.

The practical cut of this precedent runs in two directions. AI companies can cite it when disclaiming ownership of model outputs, because it supports the position that no rights vest in the machine itself. Conversely, anyone seeking to anchor copyright in an AI system's output faces the same wall. What the case does not resolve is where rights do land when a human directs a system to produce something, a question the Ninth Circuit explicitly left open by limiting its holding to standing.

One live case, the University of Tennessee Research Foundation action against Anthropic, is indexed here as downstream context. The data does not describe its claims or status in detail, so no comparison between the two matters can be drawn from what is available.
